title: The grieving mothers
hook: women who lost children, taught by Patacara: you don't know where he came from or went (Therigatha, the five hundred)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patacara told the nuns to rinse off the road and sit. Your line was wash your feet. Did you stop and arrive before something that mattered? Today, mothers come to her carrying a grief she knows. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

No one in the poem is named except the teacher. The collection gives these verses to a great crowd of women, and what they share is the worst thing: each of them has lost a child. They come to Patacara. The stories told about her say she lost her own children too, so whatever she says, she says from inside it. She doesn't offer the usual words. She doesn't say time heals, or that they'll feel better soon. She asks a question about a road. Today, her question, and what the mothers said after they heard it.
screen: `A CROWD OF GRIEVING MOTHERS.` → `A TEACHER WHO LOST HER OWN.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT A ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Patacara says, in substance: you don't know the road he came by, or the road he left by. You don't know where he came from, or where he went. And still you cry out, my son. Second, the turn. If you knew his road, she says, where he came from and where he went, you would not grieve like this. This is how it is for living beings. Third, the picture. He came without being asked, she says, and he left without asking leave. He came from somewhere and stayed a few days. From here he went one way, and from there another. Read slowly, it's the image of a traveler who stopped at your house. Fourth, what the mothers answer. In the poem they speak as one: she has drawn out the arrow lodged in my heart, the one so hard to see. She has taken away my grief for my son. Notice what Patacara does not say. She doesn't say the child didn't matter, or that the love was a mistake. Some readers hear the verses as hard, almost cold. Others hear a release: a mother told that her child's life ran longer than the few days she was given to see. And the arrow matters. An arrow is something lodged in you by no choice of your own, and something that can be drawn out. The poem never blames the mothers for carrying it. A woman who had carried it herself is the one who pulls it free.
screen: `WHERE DID HE COME FROM?` · `IF YOU KNEW HIS ROAD.` · `A TRAVELER WHO STAYED A FEW DAYS.` · `THE HIDDEN ARROW, DRAWN OUT.` · then, large: `WHERE HE CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a parent who has lost a child. This one asks for gentleness, with them and with yourself. If you are that parent, simply sit with your child's name, and let the breath come and go at its own pace. Nothing more is asked. If you know such a parent, bring them to mind: their face, their kitchen, the way they say the name. You don't need to fix anything. Just hold them in attention, the way Patacara stood with the mothers who came to her. Later, if it feels right, you might send a short note that says you remembered. The bell holds the time.
The grieving mothers. Women who came to Patacara with the loss of a child, and heard her ask where he came from and where he went. Today's word.
Your line: where he came from. Today, when you think of someone you've lost, let your mind travel back before you met them, and on past where you could follow. Day seven hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Theravada teachers can draw on Patacara's story and verses when they speak about grief, and Theravada memorial customs include chanting and offerings made in the name of the one who has died.

match.prompt: Patacara and the mothers: tap the pairs.
pairs: where did he come from, where did he go?

myth: Patacara tells the mothers that loving the child was the mistake
she says nothing like that. she asks where the child came from and where he went.
the mothers say an arrow was drawn out of their hearts
in the poem they say she pulled out the hidden arrow of grief for a son.
Patacara tells them time will heal it
she offers no such promise. she asks about the road the child came by and left by.

fork.setup: you're one of the mothers. Patacara has just asked where your son came from, and where he went. what do you say?
options: she can't know what this is like.
she has drawn out the arrow lodged in my heart.
fork.reveal: in the poem the mothers answer as one: she has drawn out the hidden arrow lodged in the heart, and taken away grief for a son.

original.note: Pali salla: an arrow or dart. The mothers say Patacara drew the hidden arrow of grief from their hearts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad poem about loss.
what it means: Patacara asks grieving mothers about the road the child came by and left by, and they say an arrow has been drawn from their hearts.
what a scholar hears: salla, the arrow of grief, appears elsewhere in the Pali texts too, as in the Salla Sutta of the Sutta Nipata, a teaching on lamenting the dead.

sources.ref: Therigatha 6.1 (Pancasatamatta, Patacara's five hundred: her verses to the grieving mothers and their reply)

notes: All Therigatha material is paraphrased; no translation quoted.
The index says 'the five hundred' (the poem's heading, Pancasata Patacara); the script says 'a great crowd of women' instead of the number. Confirm.

'The stories told about her say she lost her own children' rests on the commentary and on the verses about a bereaved woman in Kisa Gotami's poem (Thig 10.1), which the commentary connects with Patacara. Confirm the hedged phrasing.

Confirm the paraphrase of Thig 6.1: not knowing the road he came by or left by; 'if you knew... you would not grieve'; such is the nature of beings; came unasked, left without leave, stayed a few days; the mothers' reply about the hard-to-see arrow drawn out. Some translations render the child as 'son'; the script uses 'son' in the mothers' words.
'Some readers hear the verses as hard... others hear a release' is the writer's framing of differing responses; Keeper may prefer a traditional reading.
howItsDone describes memorial chanting and offerings in general terms; confirm.
Practice is sensitive: it addresses bereaved parents directly and asks nothing of them beyond sitting with the child's name. Confirm the tone.
Original: सल्ल (salla); confirm Devanagari and pronunciation guide.
Editor pass: fork rewritten from the mothers' side; the old fork (you're Patacara, a grieving mother comes, what do you say) repeated day 758's fork almost word for word. Hook closing line varied.
Audit: source ref corrected from Thig 6.2 (Vasetthi) to Thig 6.1 (Pancasatamatta, verses 127-132).
